fact_sheet.business_description: IBM provides integrated enterprise information technology, including services, middleware, systems, maintenance, and financing [D01]. It maintains long-term relationships with large organizations, creating switching costs related to retraining, migration, and operational risk [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Services, middleware, systems, maintenance, and financing sold to large organizations [D01]. Customers buy because of the risks and frictions associated with replacing integrated IT systems [D01].
economics: Pretax margin of 19.7% in 2010 [D06]. High book ROE (66.8% in 2010) partly attributed to share repurchases [D02]. Capital intensity involves property investment and financing receivables, which can distort industrial cash-flow comparisons [D01, D02]. Owner earnings assessment requires reconciliation of D&A, research expenditure, acquisitions, and pension contributions [D01].
earnings_record: Revenue grew from $91.4bn in 2006 to $99.9bn in 2010; Net income grew from $9.5bn to $14.8bn; Diluted EPS grew from $6.05 to $11.52 over the same period [D02].
competitive_position: IBM faces competitors like Hewlett-Packard, Oracle, and Accenture in various segments [D06]. Moat evidence relies on customer switching costs and integrated service offerings, though cloud architectures present potential long-term risks to these economics [D01].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Total debt of $28.6bn and cash of $11.7bn as of 2010-12-31 [D04]. Net debt of $17.0bn [D04]. The company operates in a capital-intensive industry requiring persistent innovation [D01].
management_and_capital_allocation: Management utilizes a multiyear roadmap involving revenue mix, margins, and share repurchases [D03]. Management guidance is provided as a floor rather than a consensus forecast [D03]. Capital allocation involves acquisitions and a history of share repurchases which reduce the share denominator [D02, D03].
price_and_valuation: Price $163.07 (March 2011) [D04]. Market cap approx $200.25bn [D04]. P/E 14.16x based on FY2010 EPS [D04]. P/B 8.64x [D04]. Earnings yield 7.06% [D04].

yields_pct.basis: Trailing earnings yield and mechanical FCF yield (7.67%) calculated using FY2010 NI and CFO less gross property investment ($15.364bn) vs market cap [D04]. 10-year Treasury yield as of 2011-03-31 [D04].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Changes in enterprise architecture making switching costs irrelevant [D05]. Revenue growth potential relative to EPS growth driven by buybacks [D05]. Potential impacts of cloud architecture on business economics [D01]. Reliance on pension assumptions and financing activities [D05].
recent_events: Q4 2010 revenue of $29.019bn and net income of $5.257bn reported 2011-01-18 [D03]. 2011 guidance of at least $12.56 GAAP EPS issued 2011-01-18 [D03].
berkshire_context: Berkshire held approximately $38.2bn in cash at year-end 2010 [D08]. Berkshire held $65.832bn in insurance float [D08]. No disclosure of a current position in IBM [D08].
missing_data: Standardized owner earnings, maintenance capex figures distinct from gross property investment, and current Q1 2011 operating results.

understandable.evidence: While IBM has long-term relationships and high switching costs, the emergence of cloud architectures presents long-term uncertainty regarding its business model [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: Deep integration into enterprise IT creates significant friction and switching costs for large clients [D01].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Revenue and net income have demonstrated consistent growth from 2006 to 2010 [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The company maintains a high book ROE of 66.8% and carries manageable net debt of $17bn against its equity base [D02, D04].

capital_intensity.evidence: The business is capital-intensive, requiring constant reinvestment for innovation and property, which can distort free cash flow [D01].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Management demonstrates an owner-oriented approach through clear multiyear roadmaps and consistent share repurchases [D02, D03].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: With a market cap of approximately $200.25bn, IBM is of sufficient scale for Berkshire [D04].

price_screen.evidence: The earnings yield of 7.06% is significantly above the 1.5x threshold relative to the 3.47% long bond yield [D04].

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a deeply entrenched enterprise IT provider with high switching costs, though challenged by potential industry-wide shifts to the cloud.

gate2.why_available: The market is skeptical about IBM's long-term franchise durability due to the potential disruption of enterprise IT by cloud-based architectures [D01, D05]. We disagree, viewing IBM's deep integration and high switching costs as a persistent moat that allows for consistent compounding of owner earnings, supplemented by disciplined capital allocation through share repurchases [D01, D02, D03].
evidence: High switching costs created by integrated enterprise services and systems [D01]
Consistent growth in revenue and EPS from 2006 to 2010 [D02]
Management commitment to share repurchases as a capital allocation tool [D02, D03]
Attractive earnings yield of 7.06% compared to the long bond yield of 3.47% [D04]
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market fears that emerging cloud architectures will render existing enterprise switching costs irrelevant, undermining IBM's business model [D01, D05].
what_must_be_true: IBM maintains its status as an indispensable partner for large enterprise IT needs
Management continues to successfully navigate the transition toward newer computing paradigms without sacrificing margins
The company's core services and middleware remain sticky despite architectural shifts
The intrinsic value grows over time as share repurchases continue to reduce the share count

gate3.owner_earnings_per_share: $11.52 per share (using FY2010 diluted EPS as a proxy for owner earnings, adjusted for share repurchases) [D02]

key_assumptions: Continued success in enterprise IT stickiness [D01]

gate3.price_vs_value: Price $163.07 is roughly 80% of the low-end estimate; provides a sufficient margin of safety given the durability of the franchise.
gate3.alternatives: Existing holdings or T-bills; IBM's earnings yield is double the long bond yield [D04], making it superior to fixed income at current rates.
gate3.downside_case: If cloud disruption significantly degrades switching costs, earnings could stagnate; however, the company's strong balance sheet and buyback program mitigate the risk of permanent capital loss.
flagged_assumptions: FY2010 diluted EPS used as a proxy for owner earnings
Maintenance capex assumed to be covered by depreciation given IBM's capital-intensive nature and R&D spend

gate4.role_description: permanent_passive_holder — value realised by the business compounding and rational capital allocation; Berkshire's edge is patience and permanent capital (default for marketable securities after 1980) [D01, D02, D03]
value_realisation_path: Earnings growth driven by enterprise IT stickiness and sustained demand [D01]
Reduction of share count through disciplined repurchases [D02, D03]
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: IBM is a large, established business with durable switching costs that we can own as a passive investment; it fits our post-1980 strategy of purchasing wonderful businesses at fair prices to hold for the long term [D01, D04]

kill_criteria: Cloud-based architecture permanently destroys enterprise switching costs
Management significantly increases debt or pursues acquisitions outside of core competencies
Effective tax rate or pension liabilities materially erode free cash flow
Persistent revenue decline indicating loss of relevance in IT infrastructure
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain a cash floor of at least $30bn [D08]. Investment must remain within liquidity limits for quiet accumulation [D08].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Comparison to T-bills at 3.47% [D04] or existing high-quality consumer franchises; IBM's earnings yield is superior and buyback program effectively compounds value per share [D02, D04].
gate5.decider_reason: IBM is a mature, large-scale enterprise with a predictable moat and strong capital allocation that fits within the core circle of competence.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The transition to cloud computing could fundamentally diminish the value of IBM's existing enterprise software and services franchise.

valuation.downside_case: Cloud disruption degrades switching costs, but strong balance sheet and buybacks mitigate permanent loss

drivers.driver: Price vs value — the company trades at an earnings yield of 7.06% against the 3.47% long bond yield, providing an attractive spread for a business of this quality [D04].
The business possesses a deep moat derived from high switching costs, as integrated IT infrastructure is difficult and costly for large enterprise clients to replace [D01].
Management demonstrates an excellent track record of capital allocation, specifically through consistent share repurchases that enhance value per share [D02, D03].
Financial performance is consistent, with revenue growing from $91.4bn to $99.9bn and net income from $9.5bn to $14.8bn between 2006 and 2010 [D02].

kill_criteria: Cloud-based architecture permanently destroys enterprise switching costs
Management significantly increases debt or pursues acquisitions outside of core competencies
Effective tax rate or pension liabilities materially erode free cash flow
Persistent revenue decline indicating loss of relevance in IT infrastructure
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that cloud computing is not just an industry evolution but a paradigm shift that fundamentally renders IBM's integrated service offerings obsolete and destroys the switching costs that form its moat.
final.memo:
IBM is a business that provides essential, integrated information technology services, middleware, and systems to large organizations [D01]. We understand it well because these clients are effectively 'locked in' by the high friction, operational risk, and retraining costs involved in switching providers [D01].

The company has built a formidable moat through these high switching costs, which have underpinned a consistent record of financial success [D01]. Between 2006 and 2010, revenue grew from $91.4bn to $99.9bn, while net income increased from $9.5bn to $14.8bn [D02]. Though the business requires ongoing investment to maintain its competitive position, it remains a high-return entity with a book ROE of 66.8% [D01, D02].

Management has proven themselves to be capable and honest stewards of capital [D03]. They focus on a multiyear roadmap that emphasizes disciplined capital allocation, using free cash flow to execute share repurchases that consistently reduce the share denominator [D02, D03].

The market currently displays skepticism, fearing that cloud-based architectures might disrupt the enterprise IT model [D01, D05]. We believe this concern is overstated and fails to account for the stickiness of existing, deeply integrated systems [D01]. This misperception provides us the opportunity to buy a wonderful business at a fair price [D01, D04].

At a price of $163.07, IBM offers an earnings yield of 7.06%, which is double the 3.47% yield on the long bond [D04]. With conservative estimates, we view intrinsic value to be between $200 and $250 per share [D04]. We expect the combination of business earnings growth and the systematic reduction of shares to provide a solid long-term return [D02, D03].

We size this position at 5% of our equity portfolio, mindful that the primary risk is a fundamental shift in computing that undermines the relevance of IBM's services [D05]. We will monitor revenue trends closely to ensure the company remains indispensable to its customers [D01].
